title: Henry IV, Part 1
author: William Shakespeare
setting: England and Wales in 1402 and 1403, from the Boar's-Head in Eastcheap to the field at Shrewsbury
lengthNote: Around 3,000 lines, with the Eastcheap scenes carrying an unusually large body of prose for a history play
openingLine: So shaken as we are, so wan with care, Find we a time for frighted peace to pant,
summary: A king who took the crown from Richard II cannot get out of England to atone for it, because the men who helped him take it now want paying. His heir is drinking in Eastcheap with a fat knight who thinks honour is a word, while the son of the rebel earls is winning the reputation the prince should have. The play cuts between court, tavern and rebel camp until all three arrive on the same field, and lets Hal settle the account in person.

sourceText.label: Globe/Moby text of Henry IV, Part 1
sourceText.note: Line numbers follow the traditional Globe numbering, which counts prose lines as printed. Modern editions vary.

atAGlance.label: Written
atAGlance.note: After Richard II and before the second part, which begins where this one stops.

atAGlance.label: First printed
atAGlance.note: Entered in the Stationers' Register on 25 February and printed in quarto; a fragment of an earlier printing survives.

atAGlance.label: Chief sources
atAGlance.note: With the Tudor dynastic framing of Hall behind it, and an anonymous older play, The Famous Victories, somewhere in the background.

atAGlance.label: A name changed
atAGlance.note: Traces in the text suggest the knight first carried the name of a Protestant martyr with powerful descendants.

structure.label: Act I
structure.title: The king, the tavern and the rebels
structure.summary: The king postpones his crusade because Wales and Scotland are both in flames, and envies Northumberland the son he has. Hal robs a coach with Falstaff and then tells the audience, alone, that the whole tavern life is a calculated eclipse. Hotspur refuses to hand over his prisoners and the Percys begin to plan.

scenes.title: The crusade deferred
scenes.summary: News from Wales and Northumberland cancels the king's journey to Jerusalem before it starts.

scenes.title: Eastcheap
scenes.summary: Falstaff and Hal trade insults, Poins proposes the Gadshill trick, and Hal explains his plan to nobody but us.

scenes.title: The prisoners
scenes.summary: Hotspur’s account of the popinjay on the battlefield does not save him; Worcester makes a quarrel into a conspiracy.

structure.label: Act II
structure.title: Gadshill, and the play extempore
structure.summary: Carriers, chamberlains and thieves fill the road to Gadshill, and the practical joke goes exactly as Poins designed it. Back at the tavern Falstaff's lie grows from two men to eleven while the audience counts, and then the two of them take turns playing the king so that Hal can hear his own reckoning read out in advance.

scenes.title: The inn yard at Rochester
scenes.summary: Carriers complain about fleas and the price of oats; Gadshill arranges his intelligence.

scenes.title: The highway
scenes.summary: Falstaff robs the travellers and is robbed in turn by Hal and Poins in disguise.

scenes.title: Warkworth
scenes.summary: Hotspur reads a letter of refusal aloud and refuses to tell his wife where he is going.

scenes.title: The Boar's-Head
scenes.summary: Francis is baited, the buckram men multiply, the sheriff knocks, and Falstaff is banished in play.

structure.label: Act III
structure.title: The rebels at Bangor, and the king and Hal
structure.summary: At Bangor the rebels divide England on a map and quarrel about the course of a river, and Glendower and Hotspur cannot be in a room together for ten lines. In London the king tells his son that a crown is kept by being rarely seen, and compares him — to his face — with Richard II. Hal promises to redeem everything on Percy's head.

scenes.title: The map
scenes.summary: Mortimer, Glendower, Worcester and Hotspur carve up the kingdom and argue over a bend in the Trent.

scenes.title: The interview
scenes.summary: Henry accuses Hal of being the new Richard; Hal answers with a promise and gets a command.

scenes.title: The reckoning
scenes.summary: Falstaff quarrels with the Hostess over a picked pocket and is given a charge of foot.

structure.label: Act IV
structure.title: The rebellion thins out
structure.summary: Northumberland is sick, Glendower cannot raise his men in time, and Hotspur decides that fighting without them will look better anyway. Falstaff marches a company of scarecrows he has recruited for the bribes, and admits it. The king offers terms that Worcester decides not to repeat.

scenes.title: The rebel camp
scenes.summary: Two allies fail to arrive, and Hotspur converts each absence into an argument for attacking.

scenes.title: The road near Coventry
scenes.summary: Falstaff explains, to the audience, how he sold the men who could afford to buy their way out.

scenes.title: Terms offered
scenes.summary: Blunt brings the king's offer of pardon; Hotspur recites the Percys' grievances back to the beginning.

scenes.title: York
scenes.summary: The Archbishop sends letters, expecting the rebellion to fail and the reprisals to reach him.

structure.label: Act V
structure.title: Shrewsbury
structure.summary: Worcester suppresses the king's pardon, so the battle happens on a lie. Decoy kings are killed across the field while the real one is saved by his son. Hal kills Hotspur, speaks over him with unexpected tenderness, and then watches Falstaff claim the body and the credit.

scenes.title: The catechism
scenes.summary: Hal offers single combat, the king offers pardon, and Falstaff, left alone, takes honour apart word by word.

scenes.title: The suppressed offer
scenes.summary: Worcester keeps the pardon from Hotspur, who hears instead how handsomely the prince praised him.

scenes.title: Counterfeit kings
scenes.summary: Blunt dies dressed as the king; Falstaff offers Hal a bottle of sack instead of a pistol.

scenes.title: Two stars
scenes.summary: Hal saves his father, kills Hotspur, and finds Falstaff playing dead and then claiming the kill.

scenes.title: After
scenes.summary: Worcester is sent to execution, Douglas is freed, and the king divides his armies for the campaigns still to come.

characters.name: Prince Hal
characters.role: Henry, Prince of Wales, the king's eldest son
characters.summary: He tells the audience his whole strategy in his first scene alone, which leaves the play free to spend four acts on the question of whether a man can perform disgrace for years without being changed by it. He is funnier than Falstaff intends him to be and colder than the tavern realises.
characters.clue: He explains his entire plan in a soliloquy before the audience has had time to like him, then goes back to drinking for two more acts.

relationships.label: companion, straight man and eventual judge of
relationships.note: Every scene between them rehearses the rejection that closes Part 2.

characters.name: Sir John Falstaff
characters.role: A knight, and the prince's tavern companion
characters.summary: He lies on a scale that is meant to be caught, steals from the poor and from the king's press with equal cheerfulness, and produces the only argument in the play against dying for a word. He is not a fool and he is not harmless: the hundred and fifty men he recruits for bribes are dead by Act V, and he says so himself.
characters.clue: Two men in buckram become eleven while he talks, and he stabs a corpse in the thigh to make sure of the credit.

characters.name: Hotspur
characters.role: Henry Percy, son of the Earl of Northumberland
characters.summary: He cannot finish a sentence about politics without making it a sentence about himself, and the speed is his charm and his defect. Shakespeare makes him Hal's age, which the chronicles do not, so that the play can set two versions of one generation against each other.
characters.clue: He will not hand over his prisoners, mocks a lord's perfumed handkerchief on a battlefield, and dies in the middle of his own sentence.

characters.name: King Henry IV
characters.role: King of England, formerly Henry Bolingbroke
characters.summary: He opens the play trying to leave the country on crusade and never manages it in this play or the next. His advice to his son is about being seen, not about virtue (a crown is kept by rationing it), which tells an audience exactly how he got it.
characters.clue: He wishes a fairy had swapped his son in the cradle for the rebel earl's, and says so to the lords of the council.

characters.name: Earl of Worcester
characters.summary: He is the cold intelligence behind a hot nephew, and the one man who understands that a pardon offered to the Percys would be honoured for Hotspur and not for him. Suppressing the king's offer is the single most consequential decision in the play, and he takes it in a short, entirely rational speech.
characters.clue: He decides that his own head is worth more than the truth, and keeps a pardon in his pocket while men march.

characters.name: Owen Glendower
characters.summary: He claims the earth shook at his birth and that he can call spirits, and the play neither proves nor disproves him — it simply has Hotspur laugh. He is also the one character with a household, a language and a daughter who sings, which makes the Welsh scene the play's only picture of home.
characters.clue: He says the front of heaven was full of fiery shapes when he was born, and is told that the same thing would have happened if his mother's cat had kittened.

characters.name: Lady Percy
characters.summary: She describes her husband's sleep — the muttered orders, the sweat, the starting awake — in the most precise account of a soldier's mind the play contains, and he answers by refusing to tell her anything. Their scene together is affectionate, funny and entirely one-sided about information.
characters.clue: She has watched her husband cry out about basilisks and cannon in his sleep for a fortnight, and still cannot get a straight answer out of him.

characters.name: Ned Poins
characters.summary: He invents the Gadshill counter-robbery, which is the mechanism that lets Hal watch Falstaff lie and then correct him with evidence. He is the prince’s accomplice more than his friend, and the play drops him without comment once the joke has served its purpose.
characters.clue: He is the one who works out that two men in disguise can rob the robbers and then simply listen to the story afterwards.

characters.name: Earl of Douglas
characters.role: A Scottish lord, Hotspur's prisoner and then his ally
characters.summary: He spends the battle killing men dressed as the king and getting angrier each time, which makes the play’s theme of counterfeiting into a running joke with corpses in it. He is released without ransom at the end, in the only unambiguously generous act anyone performs.
characters.clue: He keeps killing the king and keeps being told that this was not the king.

themes.name: Honour
themes.summary: The play sets three definitions against each other and refuses to arbitrate. For Hotspur honour is a thing you go and fetch from the moon or the sea floor; for Hal it is an account that can be transferred from one man's head to another; for Falstaff it is a word, air, and no use whatever to the man who died on Wednesday.
themes.development: Hotspur defines it in 1.3, Hal treats it as bookkeeping in 3.2, Falstaff takes it apart in 5.1, and in 5.4 a corpse is stabbed to claim it.

themes.name: Legitimacy
themes.summary: Henry IV holds the throne by the method his enemies are now using against him, and everybody in the play knows it. The rebels' grievance is not ideological: they helped him to the crown and were not paid, so the rebellion is a debt collection.
themes.development: The crusade that would expiate Richard's death is postponed in 1.1, the Percys recite their part in the usurpation in 4.3, and the fighting settles nothing beyond this season.

themes.name: Fathers and sons
themes.summary: Hal has three fathers in the play: the king who envies another man's child, the knight who sits in a chair with a cushion for a crown, and Hotspur's father, who does not turn up. The tavern game in 2.4 is the only interview in which the prince is allowed to answer back, and he takes both parts of it.
themes.development: Henry wishes his son exchanged in 1.1, Falstaff plays him in 2.4, and Hal is finally arraigned in earnest in 3.2 and answers with a promise about Percy.

themes.name: Performance and counterfeiting
themes.summary: Almost everyone in the play is playing someone: a prince playing a wastrel, a knight playing a king, four knights dressed as Henry IV, a dead man playing dead. The word 'counterfeit' does the heavy lifting in Act V, where it means a forged coin, an impersonation and a corpse in the same twenty lines.
themes.development: Hal announces the performance in 1.2, Falstaff and Hal rehearse a royal interview in 2.4, and the battle in 5.3 and 5.4 is fought against and by imitations.

themes.name: Time, debt and redemption
themes.summary: Falstaff's first question is what time of day it is, and the play never stops keeping accounts: reckonings in taverns, reckonings of honour, a debt owed to God, a promise to pay back time misspent. 'Redeem' is used as a commercial word before it is used as a moral one.
themes.development: Hal promises in 1.2 to pay a debt he never promised, redeems it on Percy’s head in 3.2, and in 5.1 Falstaff will not settle with a creditor who has not called.

themes.name: A country in parts
themes.summary: The play moves between court, tavern, inn yard, Welsh hall and rebel camp, and each has its own speech: royal blank verse, Eastcheap prose, carriers talking about oats and fleas, a song in Welsh nobody on stage translates. The kingdom being fought over is shown as a set of places that do not understand each other.
themes.development: The rebels literally divide it on a map in 3.1 and argue about a river; by 5.5 the king is splitting his own armies to go north and west together.

techniques.name: Prose against verse
techniques.definition: Using the shift between metrical speech and prose to mark who is speaking and where.
techniques.inThisBook: Hal moves between the two at will, which is the clearest evidence in the play that his tavern life is a costume: nobody else in Eastcheap can speak the court's language, and nobody at court can speak Falstaff's.

techniques.name: The play extempore
techniques.definition: Characters improvising a scene inside the scene they are already in.
techniques.inThisBook: In 2.4 Falstaff and Hal take turns as king and prince with a cushion for a crown, and the rehearsal predicts both the interview in 3.2 and the rejection at the end of Part 2.

techniques.name: Foil structure
techniques.definition: Building characters as deliberate answers to one another.
techniques.inThisBook: Hal stands between Hotspur, who has too much honour, and Falstaff, who has none, and the cutting between scenes keeps putting the three of them in the same frame.

techniques.name: Comic inflation
techniques.definition: A lie or a boast that grows by measurable stages while an audience keeps count.
techniques.inThisBook: Two men in buckram become four, then seven, then nine, then eleven, and the joke works because Shakespeare gives the audience the true figure before Falstaff starts.

techniques.name: Soliloquy
techniques.definition: A character alone on stage, speaking directly to the audience.
techniques.inThisBook: Hal's in 1.2 is unusual for arriving too early: it hands over the whole plan before the audience has decided how to feel about him, and Falstaff's in 5.1 answers it from the other end of the moral scale.

techniques.name: Sun and eclipse imagery
techniques.definition: A ruling image used to describe political visibility.
techniques.inThisBook: Hal imitates the sun behind clouds in 1.2, and his father in 3.2 describes his own rise in exactly the same terms of rationed appearance — father and son share a metaphor without ever comparing notes.

quotations.text: So shaken as we are, so wan with care, Find we a time for frighted peace to pant, And breathe short-winded accents of new broils To be commenced in strands afar remote.
quotations.speaker: King Henry IV
quotations.context: The opening lines of the play, announcing a crusade to Jerusalem.
quotations.analysis: The kingdom is described as a body out of breath, and the sentence itself is short-winded, breaking into clauses that never get to the main proposal. By the end of the scene the crusade has been cancelled, so the play's first policy is abandoned inside fifty lines.

quotations.text: I know you all, and will awhile uphold The unyoked humour of your idleness: Yet herein will I imitate the sun, Who doth permit the base contagious clouds To smother up his beauty from the world,
quotations.speaker: Prince Hal
quotations.context: Alone, immediately after agreeing to the Gadshill robbery.
quotations.analysis: The tense does the damage: 'will uphold' means he is choosing to keep company he has already judged. Putting this soliloquy in the first tavern scene means an audience watches every later joke knowing it is being kept for a purpose, which is why the play can be very funny and never entirely comfortable.

quotations.text: If all the year were playing holidays, To sport would be as tedious as to work; But when they seldom come, they wish'd for come, And nothing pleaseth but rare accidents.
quotations.speaker: Prince Hal
quotations.context: The middle of the same soliloquy.
quotations.analysis: Pleasure is explained as a matter of scarcity management, which is the theory of kingship his father will set out in 3.2 applied to a tavern. The balance of ‘playing holidays’ against ‘work’ also admits that Hal finds Eastcheap hard work, which nothing in his behaviour there suggests.

quotations.text: So honour cross it from the north to south, And let them grapple: O, the blood more stirs To rouse a lion than to start a hare!
quotations.speaker: Hotspur
quotations.context: Interrupting his uncle's careful explanation of the conspiracy.
quotations.analysis: Worcester is trying to lay out a plan and Hotspur answers with hunting. The two animals are the whole of his politics: he cannot imagine an opponent worth less than a lion, and the play will kill him partly because he refuses to notice the hares around him — an absent father, an unarrived ally.

quotations.text: By heaven, methinks it were an easy leap, To pluck bright honour from the pale-faced moon, Or dive into the bottom of the deep, Where fathom-line could never touch the ground, And pluck up drowned honour by the locks;
quotations.speaker: Hotspur
quotations.context: Still ignoring Worcester, in the same speech.
quotations.analysis: Honour is treated as an object with a physical location, and both locations are unreachable by design — the moon and a depth past any sounding line. Dragging a drowned thing up by the hair is a grim image for a young man's ideal, and it is the closest the play comes to predicting how he will look at Shrewsbury.

quotations.text: A plague of all cowards, I say, and a vengeance too! marry, and amen! Give me a cup of sack, boy.
quotations.speaker: Falstaff
quotations.context: Arriving at the Boar's-Head after running away at Gadshill.
quotations.analysis: He comes through the door with an accusation already in flight, which is the technique of his whole defence: attack first and let the details arrive later. The order for sack in the same breath sets the rhythm of the scene — moral outrage and refreshment, alternating, for three hundred lines.

quotations.text: O monstrous! eleven buckram men grown out of two!
quotations.speaker: Prince Hal
quotations.context: Keeping count while Falstaff describes the robbery.
quotations.analysis: Hal supplies the arithmetic the audience has been doing silently, which is why the line always gets its laugh. It also shows the pattern of their friendship: Falstaff invents and Hal audits, and every one of their scenes ends with the accounts being read back to him.

quotations.text: banish plump Jack, and banish all the world.
quotations.speaker: Falstaff
quotations.context: Playing Hal in the improvised interview, pleading his own case in the prince's voice.
quotations.analysis: He has manoeuvred himself into speaking the prince’s lines, so the plea for his own life comes out of Hal’s mouth by proxy. ‘All the world’ is an accurate description of what the tavern scenes contain, carriers, drawers, hostesses, thieves, none of whom survives into the reign that follows.

quotations.text: I do, I will.
quotations.speaker: Prince Hal
quotations.context: Answering, in the king's part, Falstaff's plea not to be banished.
quotations.analysis: Four words, two tenses, and the whole of Part 2 in the second one. The present tense keeps it inside the game, the future steps outside it, and the knocking at the door arrives immediately afterwards so that nobody on stage has to decide which he meant.

quotations.text: Why, so can I, or so can any man; But will they come when you do call for them?
quotations.speaker: Hotspur
quotations.context: Answering Glendower's claim that he can call spirits from the vasty deep.
quotations.analysis: The reply does not deny magic; it wants evidence that the spirits turn up, which is a joke about rebellion as much as about sorcery. The two men are at this moment allies who have between them neither Northumberland's army nor Glendower's, so the question lands on the alliance itself.

quotations.text: O, while you live, tell truth and shame the devil!
quotations.speaker: Hotspur
quotations.context: Ending the argument with Glendower over the map at Bangor.
quotations.analysis: It is a proverb, delivered as if newly minted, by a man who cannot hear a boast without correcting it. The line is worth setting beside Falstaff at the Boar's-Head: this play's two most attractive characters are the one who cannot stop lying and the one who cannot stop calling it out.

quotations.text: Had I so lavish of my presence been, So common-hackney'd in the eyes of men, So stale and cheap to vulgar company, Opinion, that did help me to the crown, Had still kept loyal to possession
quotations.speaker: King Henry IV
quotations.context: Lecturing Hal on why Richard II lost the throne.
quotations.analysis: The king's theory of power is entirely about supply: appear rarely and you are valued, appear often and you are spent. He also lets slip the true basis of his title in a single word — 'Opinion' helped him to the crown, not God or law — which is the most honest sentence he speaks in either part.

quotations.text: Percy is but my factor, good my lord, To engross up glorious deeds on my behalf; And I will call him to so strict account, That he shall render every glory up,
quotations.speaker: Prince Hal
quotations.context: Promising his father that he will take Hotspur's reputation.
quotations.analysis: A factor is an agent who buys goods for someone else, so Hal casts his rival as an employee who has been accumulating stock on his account. Honour here is audited, not fought for, and the vocabulary is the tavern’s, reckonings, accounts, rendering up, applied to a battlefield.

quotations.text: The land is burning; Percy stands on high; And either we or they must lower lie.
quotations.speaker: Prince Hal
quotations.context: The last words of the tavern scene in Act III, spoken to Falstaff before leaving for the wars.
quotations.analysis: Hal drops into rhyme to exit, and Falstaff's first response is to call it rare words and order breakfast. The couplet marks the point where the prince starts speaking in the register of the campaign and the knight declines to follow him into it.

quotations.text: Tut, tut; good enough to toss; food for powder, food for powder; they'll fill a pit as well as better: tush, man, mortal men, mortal men.
quotations.speaker: Falstaff
quotations.context: Westmoreland has just remarked how wretched Falstaff's recruits look.
quotations.analysis: The repetitions are the sound of a man who has already settled the question and is now only soothing an objection. He has taken bribes from the men who could pay and marched the ones who could not, and 'mortal men' converts an admission of fraud into a piece of philosophy about death in general.

quotations.text: The Prince of Wales doth join with all the world In praise of Henry Percy: by my hopes, This present enterprise set off his head, I do not think a braver gentleman, More active-valiant or more valiant-young, More daring or more bold, is now alive
quotations.speaker: Prince Hal
quotations.context: Offering, before the king and the rebel envoy, to fight Hotspur in single combat.
quotations.analysis: The praise is public, generous and tactically perfect: it makes the challenge impossible to refuse without loss. Vernon repeats it to Hotspur in the next act, and the report of it moves Hotspur more than the pardon that Worcester has just suppressed.

quotations.text: Why, thou owest God a death.
quotations.speaker: Prince Hal
quotations.context: Falstaff has just asked Hal to stand over him if he falls in the battle.
quotations.analysis: The commonplace is delivered as a piece of bookkeeping — a death is a debt, and debts are what this friendship runs on. Falstaff answers that it is not due yet and he would be loath to pay before the day, treating death as a bill he means to dispute, and leading straight into the catechism on honour.

quotations.text: Honour hath no skill in surgery, then? no. What is honour? a word. What is in that word honour? what is that honour? air. A trim reckoning! Who hath it? he that died o' Wednesday.
quotations.speaker: Falstaff
quotations.context: Alone on stage before the battle, in the speech he calls his catechism.
quotations.analysis: He conducts it as a catechism, question and answer, which is the form used to teach children the articles of faith — so the demolition of honour is carried out in the shape of a lesson in belief. 'He that died o' Wednesday' gives the abstraction a day of the week, and that is what finishes it off.

quotations.text: O gentlemen, the time of life is short!
quotations.speaker: Hotspur
quotations.context: His last speech to his men before the charge at Shrewsbury.
quotations.analysis: It is the only moment when Hotspur sounds as if he has understood something as well as felt it, and it comes twenty lines after Worcester has kept back the pardon that would have made the charge unnecessary. The play lets him have his finest line on the strength of a lie he does not know he has been told.

quotations.text: Two stars keep not their motion in one sphere; Nor can one England brook a double reign, Of Harry Percy and the Prince of Wales.
quotations.speaker: Prince Hal
quotations.context: Meeting Hotspur face to face for the first and only time.
quotations.analysis: They have never shared a scene until this moment, and the play has been arranging the comparison for four acts without letting them meet. The astronomy is courteous — two stars, not a star and a candle — and the shared first name in the last line makes the duel look briefly like a man fighting himself.

quotations.text: But thought's the slave of life, and life time's fool; And time, that takes survey of all the world, Must have a stop. O, I could prophesy, But that the earthy and cold hand of death Lies on my tongue: no, Percy, thou art dust And food for--
quotations.speaker: Hotspur
quotations.context: Dying at Hal's feet on the field at Shrewsbury.
quotations.analysis: The man who could not finish listening to anybody now cannot finish his own sentence, and Hal completes it for him with the word 'worms'. Having spent the play chasing a future, he dies mid-prophecy, and the broken line is the most eloquent piece of punctuation in the play.

quotations.text: The better part of valour is discretion; in the which better part I have saved my life.
quotations.speaker: Falstaff
quotations.context: Getting up off the battlefield after playing dead to escape Douglas.
quotations.analysis: The proverb is normally the other way round, and reversing it makes a maxim about courage into a defence of cowardice without changing the meaning of a word. It follows a short argument that a corpse is the counterfeit and a living man who fakes death is the true image of life, which is as close to a philosophy as he ever gets.

quotations.text: No, that's certain; I am not a double man: but if I be not Jack Falstaff, then am I a Jack. There is Percy:
quotations.speaker: Falstaff
quotations.context: Carrying Hotspur's body on his back, in front of a prince who saw him lying dead.
quotations.analysis: 'Double' means both a phantom and a man carrying a second body, so the denial is also a description of what the audience is looking at. Hal lets the claim stand and offers to gild the lie, which tells us more about the prince's politics than about his affection.

timeline.label: Henry Percy, called Hotspur, is born
timeline.detail: He was in fact older than Henry IV, and old enough to be Hal's father; Shakespeare makes the two young men coevals so that they can be compared.

timeline.label: Henry Bolingbroke takes the crown
timeline.detail: The deposition staged in Richard II, and the debt the Percys come to collect in this play.

timeline.label: Richard II dies in captivity
timeline.detail: The death that the crusade to Jerusalem is meant to expiate, and that the new king never gets round to atoning for.

timeline.label: Hotspur defeats the Scots at Homildon Hill
timeline.detail: The victory whose prisoners he refuses to surrender in 1.3, which begins the quarrel.

timeline.label: The battle of Shrewsbury
timeline.detail: Fought on 21 July, and won by the king; the single combat between Hal and Hotspur is Shakespeare's invention.

timeline.label: Henry IV dies and Hal becomes Henry V
timeline.detail: Two plays later, and with Falstaff still expecting to be made an earl or a duke.

timeline.label: Holinshed's Chronicles reissued
timeline.detail: The second edition is the play's principal quarry for the Percy rebellion and Shrewsbury.

timeline.label: The play is written and staged
timeline.detail: Usually dated to about this year, and probably in performance before it was entered for printing.

timeline.label: Entered in the Stationers' Register and printed
timeline.detail: Andrew Wise entered it on 25 February; Peter Short printed the quarto, whose title page advertises Shrewsbury, Hotspur and the humorous conceits of Sir John Falstaff.

timeline.label: A second quarto, newly corrected
timeline.detail: The first of a string of reprints that make this the most frequently printed of Shakespeare's plays before the Folio.

timeline.label: The First Folio
timeline.detail: Printed as The First Part of Henry the Fourth, fixing the play inside the run from Richard II to Henry V.

places.name: Eastcheap, London
places.note: The street of the Boar's-Head, and the play's second court.

places.name: Gad's Hill, near Rochester
places.note: The stretch of the Dover road where the robbery and the counter-robbery take place.

places.name: Warkworth Castle, Northumberland
places.note: The Percy stronghold where Hotspur reads a letter of refusal aloud and refuses to confide in his wife.

places.name: Bangor, Gwynedd
places.note: Where the rebels divide England on a map and argue over the course of the Trent.

places.name: Shrewsbury
places.note: The field where the play's three worlds finally meet, on 21 July 1403.

criticalViews.summary: The oldest account reads the play as a structured apprenticeship: Hal learns the whole kingdom, from carriers to kings, and earns the crown that his father only seized.
criticalViews.counter: It depends on taking the soliloquy in 1.2 at face value, and that speech shows a man who needs no education because he has already decided what the tavern is for.

criticalViews.position: A play about how power manages its own image
criticalViews.summary: Newer historicist criticism has focused on the way authority in these plays produces disorder in order to be seen putting it down, with Hal's misrule and its public correction as the model case.
criticalViews.counter: The reading can make the play airless, and it has little to say about why Falstaff is funny, which is not a trivial fact about him.

criticalViews.position: Falstaff as the play's real centre
criticalViews.summary: A long tradition, running through the eighteenth century and beyond, treats Falstaff as a comic creation too large for the history he is placed in, and reads the political plot as the frame around him.
criticalViews.counter: It can go soft on what he actually does — pressing men for bribes, marching them to be killed, stabbing a corpse — all of which the text is careful to show.

essayQuestions.question: What does the play conclude about honour?
essayQuestions.focus: Hotspur, Falstaff and the space between them
plan: Set out Hotspur's definition from 1.3: honour as an object to be fetched from an impossible place.
Set out Falstaff's from 5.1: honour as a word with no surgical use and no living owner.
Show Hal converting it into a transferable account in 3.2, which is neither of the other two positions.
Test all three against 5.4, where Hotspur dies mid-sentence, Falstaff plays dead, and the credit is claimed by the wrong man.
Decide whether the play adjudicates or simply leaves three definitions standing, and what the ending does with the man who keeps the corpse.

essayQuestions.question: Is Hal's soliloquy in 1.2 a confession, a plan or a defence?
essayQuestions.focus: Character, timing and the audience's position
plan: Note where the speech falls: after the robbery is agreed, and before the audience has seen him with anyone but Falstaff and Poins.
Read the tense and modality closely — 'I know you all', 'will awhile uphold' — and what they claim about the scenes still to come.
Set the sun and cloud imagery beside the king's advice in 3.2 and ask who learned it from whom.
Consider how the speech changes a rereading of 2.4, especially the play extempore and 'I do, I will'.
Conclude on whether the soliloquy is meant to reassure an audience about a prince, or to unsettle it about a future king.

essayQuestions.question: How does the play use the movement between court, tavern and camp?
essayQuestions.focus: Structure, register and the shape of the kingdom
plan: Chart the cutting in Acts I and II: each scene answers the one before, and 1.2 and 1.3 present two sons in succession.
Show how prose and verse mark the spaces, and how Hal is the only character who moves fluently between them.
Bring in the carriers in 2.1 and the recruits in 4.2 as the play's view from below the plot.
Use 3.1, where the rebels divide England on a map, as the moment the technique becomes the subject.
Close on Shrewsbury, where all three worlds are finally in the same place, and ask what survives the meeting.

essayQuestions.question: Does Worcester or Hotspur destroy the rebellion?
essayQuestions.focus: Political judgement and the suppressed pardon
plan: Trace Worcester's role from 1.3, where he converts a family quarrel into a conspiracy.
Set Hotspur's decisions in 4.1 against the evidence: two armies missing, and each absence turned into a reason to fight now.
Examine 5.2 in detail — the reasoning by which Worcester keeps the king's offer from his nephew, and whether it is wrong.
Weigh the effect of Vernon's report of Hal's praise, which reaches Hotspur when the pardon does not.
Judge how far the play makes the defeat a matter of character and how far a matter of one man's calculation.

discussionQuestions: Hal tells the audience his plan before we have decided whether to like him. Does that make the play more honest, or the prince harder to forgive?
Falstaff's catechism on honour comes immediately before a battle in which men he pressed for bribes are killed. Is the speech still funny?
Shakespeare makes Hotspur young, though the chronicles make him older than the king. What does the change buy the play?
Lady Percy describes her husband's sleep more accurately than anyone describes him awake. Why does the play give that speech to her?
The play ends with armies dividing for campaigns not yet fought. Is this a complete play or the first half of one?

related.why: The play immediately before: the deposition, and the debt to the Percys that this rebellion is collecting.
The sequel, where the tavern gets colder, the king finally dies, and 'I do, I will' is carried out in public.
The reign the prince has been preparing for, with the same trick of moving in disguise among ordinary soldiers.
Both parts in a single Astor volume, for reading the whole arc from Shrewsbury to the rejection in one sitting.
Falstaff transplanted into a citizen comedy, and a useful test of how much of him belongs to the history plays.
